title_original: Between Legacy and Discovery: Rebekah Sherman-Myntti on the 2026 Downtown Festival
excerpt_original: In a city like New York, what’s another film festival? When one can crop up in any neighborhood, keeping track is neither possible nor desirable. So if I might’ve accordingly raised an eyebrow to hear of the Downtown Festival upon its appearance in 2024, allow me a moment of…

blocks.text: In a city like New York, what’s another film festival? When one can crop up in any neighborhood, keeping track is neither possible nor desirable. So if I might’ve accordingly raised an eyebrow to hear of the Downtown Festival upon its appearance in 2024, allow me a moment of judging a book by its cover.

Coming to know the festival and its founder, Rebekah Sherman-Myntti, has disavowed any wonky feelings. Downtown, now in its third year, is further and further proving itself a valuable companion to New York’s larger festivals: a repository for debut filmmakers, low-budget fare, or (speaking for myself and a small group of friends) an undistributed TV pilot that was shot in our apartments and serves as something of an all-male Girls riff. It’s a place that makes artists feel welcome and comfortable, allowing them to tailor a world premiere to their desires without excluding them from a larger flux.

Sherman-Myntti and I spoke about Downtown’s third year , which commences tonight with Paul Schrader’s The Basics of Philosophy , a film she says exemplifies the festival’s balance between legacy and discovery.
Let’s start with a basic question: can you tell me how the third edition of The Downtown Festival separates itself from predecessors?

I think this year feels quite a bit different. The first two editions were really about establishing the festival’s identity and proving the concept. In 2024, I wanted to see if this seemingly crazy idea could actually work and be pulled off. In 2025, it was really about realizing how much of an appetite there was for something like this to exist, which was super exciting. With the third edition this year, the scale is much bigger, the program is more ambitious, and the relationships between film, music, artist talks, and nightlife feel way more intertwined.

At the same time, the core idea of the festival hasn’t changed. It’s still artists-for-artists, deeply rooted in discovery, and focused on creating real exchanges between filmmakers, musicians, and various other disciplines. I’m always thinking about the kind of festival experience I’d genuinely want as a filmmaker… one where people feel supported, connected to their fellow artists as well as audiences, and part of something that can continue beyond a single event. We haven’t even announced half of our non-film programming yet! So stay tuned.
The Story of Eve by Alexandra Cabral

The program is impressive, albeit not comprising much that is even the least-bit known. I’m curious, also, about the distinction between programming a number of first-time filmmakers—exactly the kind of group that would struggle to be prioritized by programmers—and films that are plainly worthwhile, regardless of author. Do you see yourself prioritizing one while still hoping to serve another?

I definitely don’t prioritize first-time filmmakers just because they’re first-time filmmakers. I like to prioritize work that feels incredibly specific and like it has a real point of view. There has to be a certain aliveness to it. With films, we’re always looking for ones that feel deeply personal, where you can really sense that the filmmaker had to make this film in this way. Rather than something that could have been made by anyone or that feels like it’s trying to fit into an existing mold.

That said: I do feel really strongly about making space for artists who haven’t already been “validated” by the usual systems. If someone has made something amazing and doesn’t yet have representation, press, institutional support, or a recognizable name attached to them, that makes me more interested. I think festivals can play a meaningful role in helping people discover work they might not otherwise know about and in giving that work a context that helps audiences understand why it’s cool or important.

At the Downtown Festival, you can have a true legend like Paul Schrader showing work alongside a visual artist making her first feature, like Ondine Viñao, and have both works taken equally seriously. You can also have someone like Paul Tschinkel, whose work is so beautifully tied to an older New York art world and to documenting artists from that era, sitting alongside much newer and younger voices. I love those kinds of juxtapositions because they break down the hierarchy a bit. The work gets to speak for itself and our audience can experience someone they already know alongside someone they may be discovering for the very first time. That tension between legacy and discovery is super fascinating to me and it’s a huge part of what makes programming exciting and fun for me and Briana. There’s so much value in putting artists who helped shape a particular cultural moment in direct conversation with people who are reinterpreting or challenging it now.
How much do you see yourself as separate from the elite New York pack of ND/NF, Tribeca, and NYFF? Is there anything you actively seek to do differently?

I definitely see us as separate, but not in an antagonistic way. Those festivals have their own incredible histories, scales, and institutional roles. I really enjoy going to screenings at them. I would say that The Downtown Festival is something very different! The biggest differentiating factor is probably that we are truly multidisciplinary. Film is a huge part of it, but it exists alongside music, artist talks, performances, and other one-night-only events. I’m interested in what happens when all of those worlds actually overlap rather than being treated as separate cultural lanes. The festival is also very multigenerational and very explicitly artists-for-artists. I want somebody making their first film to feel as meaningfully included as somebody who has been making work for forty years. We’re much less interested in reinforcing traditional hierarchies around who is already considered “important” enough to deserve attention.

And structurally, we’re an extremely tiny team and we don’t have a huge institution or infrastructure behind us. That limitation has actually shaped the festival in a way I really value because it keeps things super personal and close to the artists. I also like the flexibility and organized chaos because with that comes the freedom of spontaneity! It’s great to have the independence to occasionally make decisions quickly or very last-minute and sometimes build programs around conversations and relationships rather than around a preexisting institutional framework or schedule.

With our film program, we’re interested not only in the film and the screening itself, but in everything that forms around it: who is in the room, who engages with the work, artists meeting each other, what conversations continue afterward, and what kinds of relationships or collaborations might emerge from that experience. For me, the festival is as much about creating the conditions for genuine artistic exchange as it is about presenting a slate of films.

It’s notable that this is not The Downtown Film Festival. You have a music showcase and events sponsored by MFNY. Do you see these as in any way linked to cinema? I won’t try to force some idea of “live concerts are actually cinema,” but there’s an interesting intersection of a communal vibe to screenings and actual communal events that aren’t screenings.

Very much so. The point was never to build a film festival that just happened to have a few side events. The multidisciplinary aspect is fundamental to what The Downtown Festival is, and for me, the connective tissue is the artists and the audience. Film, music, art, performance, and nightlife all create communal experiences in different ways, and I love what happens when those artists and audiences collide. Historically, downtown New York culture wasn’t neatly divided into disciplines. Filmmakers were hanging out with musicians, visual artists were acting in and making films, musicians were making movies, and everyone was ending up in the same clubs. There was a real fluidity to it.

I’m much more interested in that kind of cross-pollination than keeping everything professionally siloed, which I think happens far too often now. Especially in a festival context. I really don’t believe in “staying in your lane.” The festival is about creating a space where those different worlds can come together naturally. And a big shoutout to MFNY for supporting that vision this year!
Without asking you to give away too much, what do you see as an expansion in future years?

I’d love for The Downtown Festival to become a true home base for artists from around the world who are making work that doesn’t fit into established categories and who are looking for a genuine community around what they make. A huge part of that is continuing to bring different generations into direct conversation with one another. I want artists to be able to show work alongside people they might never otherwise be programmed with—for those combinations to create unexpected connections between the work, the artists, and our audience. I also want to expand the festival’s footprint across downtown New York, taking over more spaces and neighborhoods all throughout Lower Manhattan. Ultimately, I see the festival as part of a much larger artistic ecosystem. I’m also a filmmaker and producer working on a few projects that connect to that broader “Downtown” world. I can’t say too much yet but there’s more coming soon.
Do you prioritize anything in particular when programming short films and music videos? Or, say, a TV pilot?

Point of view above everything. With shorts especially, I’m very resistant to the idea that they’re simply calling cards or proof-of-concepts for features. A short should justify its own form, you know? It should feel like the artist chose that length because it was exactly the right container for the idea. With a TV pilot, I’m looking for the same thing: specificity, meaning, and whether the work creates a world I want to spend time in, or at least one that feels unmistakably its own. In the case of Fellas , you guys created a world that genuinely makes me laugh, but also has a lot of heart. I’m so excited for you to share it with our audience.
Fellas by Matthew Danger Lippman

The Roxy is an interesting space to hold a festival. As a single-screen theater, there’s a big bleed-through of the crowd for something that just ended and something that’s just beginning—you genuinely can’t tell who’s who. I fear I’m answering my own question, but can you tell me what you especially like about hosting a festival there?

They have been incredible hosts of The Downtown Festival’s film program! And after a few days, Roxy Cinema starts to feel like our little clubhouse—it’s the best. I love the setup and energy there because there’s so much natural crossover. People come out of one screening and run into someone arriving for the next, filmmakers stay for other films. Everyone ends up catching up in the lobby or green room. I’ve seen real deals get made and really awesome collaborations begin there. Remind me to tell you the story about Abel [Ferrara] yelling to Susan Seidelman’s husband from inside the cinema because he wanted to stay for Abel’s film but Susan had made a dinner reservation and they needed to leave ASAP. Hilarious.

Illyse Singer, the cinema’s director, has been incredibly, incredibly supportive of me on the filmmaking side of things as well as with the festival. I love her very much. The cinema’s projectionists Mitchell [Mailloux Glidden] and Dillon [Friend] really hold it down with all of the files (a massive undertaking) and the rest of the staff are amazing. It’s also just a beautiful place to watch a movie—like watching a film inside a jewel box. It’s a very intimate setting, which is different from some larger festivals where you’re in a massive theater watching a filmmaker speak on a stage that feels very far away—physically and emotionally!
Like any proper festival director, you have a great sense of style. What do you prioritize for Downtown fits?
[Laughs] That’s really nice of you. My go-to is sequins and leather pants—I basically spend the entire festival running around dressed like Michael Jackson.
The Downtown Festival is now underway.
